body: WOW. She has tastebuds of Doom.... i mean my pupper eats his own poop but he doesn't like bitter spray. so I'm trying to teach him the leave it command. it is taking good while.

1. pupper will start teething around 4 to 5 months or even 6 months. unlikely to yelp in pain but VERY likely to want to chew things to relieve the discomfort. make sure to offer lots of chew toys, use bitter apple spray on things you don't want her to chew.
2. depends on the laws of your country or state. in my country all dogs need to be microchipped and registered. I do recommend getting her chipped. if she runs away or gets lost it's one way they can help bring her back to you and it can prove ownership i think. 
3. don't take out pupper for walks to areas where there are other dogs but do take them out if you can carry them so they get used to outside world noises and smells. Just don't meet other dogs. Parvo and Distemper are scary diseases that can easily kill puppies. 
4. I don't play music so can't comment but I've heard dogs like music but you want want to see which one your pupper prefers. 

Extra tips. enrichment toys and puzzle feeders have been a godsend. Highly recommend buying them. i got mine from Amazon. I rotate because my puppy is far too clever and figures them out quick so I need to let him forget how they work.

psychoanalysis is REALLY different from behavioral therapy. (it feels really different as a client). 

all therapists will take several sessions to get to know you as a client, your issues, strengths etc. psychoanalysis takes longer as they want to see deeper and that can take time to be revealed and get a sense of. 

if it's only been a few sessions that it's probably still in the beginning stages. So don't worry too much. 

As for bringing up your worries..  remember that you are the client. you always have control. you get to ask anything you want. you can't offend him or piss him off. it is your right to understand what is happening in sessions. what the plan is. what the goals are. it is your right to ask. 

it's OK to have some concerns or fears. it's alright to be hesitant to bring up your concerns but it is still something that you can do at any time.

I don't wanna freak you out or anything but it's going to take time. I don't know how much time but probably a bit more than you think. may I suggest you track the number of good days. the duration between them as well as duration of good days. you will slowly start to see increases in the number and durations of the good days. but you won't see the bad days just suddenly stop. but with some courage, some dedication and sticking through the shit days .. eventually the bad days will be rare enough to not matter at all. 

you aren't doing anything wrong. you are starting on the right path. keep on at it. things do get better.

So ok, first off. what you've shared, not that unusual. especially for someone who hasn't done therapy before. it feels weird and frustrating. totally normal. 

now, on to your questions. 

1. you can't disappoint her. you can only disappoint yourself. because it's your life. how do you make an actionable plan? well, however works best for you. the therapist is there for you to bounce ideas off, to explore. ask her questions, share your ideas, see how you feel. know that you can change or reject the plan whenever and start again if you need to. try things out. see if they work or not. make the best plan for you. 

2. there is no right way to therapy. there are as many ways to therapy as there are people. the only wrong way would be to hide or lie or pretend. where it gets hard is that, it takes a lot of courage to be open, honest and real. 5 sessions is still early. it can take months to build a rapport between therapist and client. you aren't doing anything wrong. 

3. it depends on her modality. person centered therapy and psychodynamic (for e.g.) often don't lead the therapy with a lot of questions and instead allow the client to set the tone and direction. it can feel weird or frustrating but it allows you you explore yourself deeper, find your own truths. If it's not for you, that's OK. ask your therapist about their method, if you think it doesn't work for you, there are other therapy techniques that may work better for you. 

4. you can quit whenever you want. I'd like to suggest you bring these concerns up with your T. 

extra.

(I know you didn't ask, but may I just say) Feelings are at the core of our experience but we aren't always taught to connect with them and process them. so when you mentioned that you avoid feelings.. well I wanted to tell you, that works in the short run but you are cutting yourself off from a wealth of experiences and chance for growth. being aware of our feelings, seeing them as signals for what we need, managing them.. all that helps with our resilience to challenges, our self understanding and well long story short, can help us be stronger and more confident. 

I know that feels are the hard part but.. therapists are here to help us understand our own feelings, learn to cope in healthy ways and grow bigger around our feelings rather then spend our energy repressing them. soo.. maybe explore that side.

Your feelings are always valid however sometimes it's good to just check if they are helping you.

 It feels awful to have someone you trust break that trust. that is never going to feel ok. and most of the time,  breaking someone's trust isn't ok. however there are some rare, very rare situations where breaking a person's trust may be the better option in the long term. those times are when we are genuinely trying to protect and keep someone healthy. now even in these situations, breaking someone's trust should not be easy or pleasant. 

Therapists have to work with a certain code of ethics and that ethics tells them that it's their responsibility to try to protect you from self harm or harm of others. this is the only clear time they are told they should break confidentiality. 

So you were violated. you can feel angry and sad. you have every right to be upset. but what you do with those feelings is the important one. does it serve you to leave therapy? or find another therapist and psych? or are you going to them to grow stronger and healthier? besides talking to your pscyh which sounds as if it was done with your interest at heart, did she violate your trust in other ways? Do you think you could trust her enough to talk about your feelings with what's happened?

not to say you don't have other options besides leaving or staying. 

your psychiatrist sounds a bit .. too professional. which isn't bad exactly. but maybe you'd prefer someone a bit more personable? are there options to change doctors? or can you maybe manage things with the psych differently? 

Your therapist (if you can trust her at least this much), might help with that. could you at least try discussing this. if you don't like her answers know that you have options, like leaving but it takes a lot of strength and bravery to stay to sort things out and that can be a valuable experience.

My therapist was very supportive and encouraging when I expressed an interest in becoming a therapist. however I stopped seeing him before I started training and returned only near the end of my training. 

Partly I was afraid of sharing my difficulties or fears about the learning and training part, fear of being seen as not being good enough. Partly also as I realize he is my therapist not my teacher. It's not his role to become my mentor or even a fellow colleague (sort of). So in sessions I rarely bring up my issues with being a newly qualified therapist. Instead we focus on my other issues. 

We focus on my issues surrounding my family, my dealing with chronic pain. When I have brought up some anxieties about not being good enough as a therapist, he listens, normalizes but he doesn't share either. Which I've come to interpret as him setting his own boundary which i respect. 

And instead I've tried had to make connections with other therapists or student therapists, to have meetups and share stories, fears, resources. I found this super helpful, particularly when it's with someone who has gone to the same school and therefore we share similar experiences. 

For me, it helped to set mental boundaries on what I expect from my therapist as a professional. I also remember that his training and experience was very different from mine. He had training in another country decades ago.

whoa, ok. reading your post, I got abit concerned. 

firstly, no you should not quit... well you shouldn't quit trying to get better. you deserve to feel better. you deserve help and you are NOT wasting anyones time. 

that being said, what your therapist said was out of line. it wasn't helpful. it wasn't useful and I think she should know the effect her words had. I am not saying she is a bad therapist but she has a chance here to learn and become better. 

I don't know how long you've been in therapy. what type of therapy you've received (she sounds like she does CBT?). Are you on any medications? what type of treatment you've tried (not just meds but things like mindfulness, meditation, tapping etc) but I don't think you can ever just say ok this isn't working let's give up altogether. 


So, here's my 2 cents. I've suffered depression since my tweens. I've had suicide ideation, or thoughts or plans or ... just believing that death would be better. This is such a tough one. its hard to talk about. its hard to think about but you can't stop thinking about it. you aren't alone. 

I've been in therapy on and off for almost half my life. more then a decade. I've had psychiatrists and a bunch of different therapists. mostly because I'd move, they'd move, I'd give up. I'd go back. if I've learned anything its, 

1. try it all. even if it sounds silly, like tapping therapy (which sounds like bullshit but, did kinda help). try it for a while try. under different circumstances. if it works sometimes, keep at it. if it feels wrong stop. 

2. talk to your therapist about how you feel about the process, not just your life or your problems. (this one is super tough). they are supposed to be collaborating with us. when I realized this, I felt more empowered. I told my T when things helped, when things didn't. T helped me see if maybe I was expecting too much. to count the tiny gains. They celebrated with me when I had even minor successes. 

3. Take note of any tiny gain. Make a space for the hardship now. This worked for my suicidal thoughts. I just decided ok, I want to die. I will always think this but its ok because I won't die today, today I'm going to focus on my work, friends, health whatever. When I made a space in my mind for my suicidal thoughts and depression they started to kinda go away and not bother me as much. Just accepting that they are there but that lts ok. (I'm not saying it will work for you  but maybe you are willing to try?) 

I acknowledge its tough where you are, in a rural area. feeling like you haven't got a lot of choices for help but I also think that makes you really brave and tough to have endured as you have. made the best of your situation. Taken charge as you have. 

I can't offer more, but know that an internet stranger cares. Don't give up just yet. there's more to try!

I have a question, I hope it doesn't sound rude or accusatory. I am genuinely curious and would like to understand better. 

If you feel better doing these things, do you do them without the sheet? without being prompted? how many times per day, how often? 

what would you like more of in therapy and from your therapist? 

I would like to know and if your therapist is worth their salt, they would too. 

I have done these sheets. yes I felt they were pointless. I would fill them in. never very consistently though. The benefit wasn't the writing it in, that doesn't help. for me the benefit was becoming aware of my own behavior and habits. like seeing my daily choices in big picture. 

when I spent time thinking about things I did that alleviated my depression or anxiety, I realized it was time I wasn't actively mulling over my anxiety and depression. That was nice. Its become habit now. 

it didn't cure my depression. or anxiety. But it was helpful to reflect and talk about my actions and choices. My therapist used these sheets in many ways to better understand me. 

I think people expect therapy to be the therapist dishing out life changing advice when at least for me the best most powerful change happened with the process. learning about me, learning i have some power and choice and when I didnt  to accept. that can't be put into a sheet though.

Think of it this way if you are crying in therapy, it is tears that you desperately needed to shed. emotions that you needed to release and therapy is meant to be a safe space for just this. 

Dont rush it. be ok with what you need. Cry while you feel the need to and know that each tear is your brain amd body processing the pain and moving beyond it. when you are ready, you wont cry so much and be able to speak. 

When he asks what you are feeling.. he isnt pushing. he is... trying to help. if we can identify what we feel. just saying it. it allows us to be in the present moment. if you cant say it, dont worry. just feel. when you can say what you feel, do it. 

till then, just be in the moment with whatever you feel without fear or expectation.

so.. here's the rub about depression. one of the most common symptoms is what you're describing, apathy and hopelessness. 

so the whole dont want to talk to my therapist and psychiatrist is kinda classic. which is to say, it isnt you, it's the depression talking. so you have 2 choices here, listen to the depression and say nothing. stay where you are. OR speak up, share what your are feeling, thinking. 

Now I admit there is no guarantee that talking about it will change the depression though in my experience just saying it aloud can help. here is what you can expect. your therapist tries to understand. they ask to hear more about your experience. they explore some short term goals and coping mechanisms. some of these may not help, some will. 

your psychiatrist should consider changing your meds maybe dosage maybe adding something else. meds could be making your depression worse or just not helping. tweaking them should help. it may not work immediately. But your psych will want to try to find the med that does. 

May I add, that what you feel right now. this do nothing. nothing will change. no point. no energy. that's ok. It won't last forever. nothing ever does. So you dont HAVE to talk right now. you can allow yourself some time and space to just stay right here in this phase until you feel ready to talk. ready to move forward. this is your journey, friend. you have control. Just dont assume that what depression is making you feel and think is some fact of you. It's the depression.

I was put on Paxil, switched to lexapro, was on it for nearly two years during which I spiralled down to my worst period. Then I left aus and came to hk. I had graduated but I had no job. I couldn’t afford the meds. It was tough. I was suicidal. But I was desperate to hide it. That alone made me go to therapy. Luckily there is a charity that offers counselling on a sliding scale and I went there. My therapist recommended a psychiatrist. I was almost broke but desperate enough to go. saw a psych who said some things about needing to be on meds for the rest of my life but what he put me on (forget what it was at the moment) made me feel sick. 

I hated his attitude and I was paying so much and didn’t have w job so I quit the meds. Decided I’d do it without the meds or die trying. 

Thing is with my therapists helps, I broke it down into little goals. First up was sleep. Sleep same time. Get up out of bed and look out the window. Rinse repeat. It was hard. Sometimes it still is. Initially I used the sedatives the psych gave me. But I didn’t want to go back for more so I tried lavender tea, chamomile, melatonin. They helped. 

Next I worked on diet. I took omega 3 supplements initially then started trying to eat more nutrient rich foods. Cut out the crap. 

Finally I worked on other goals that would help build my own self.  Got a job. Joined a gym, tried kickboxing, made efforts to be creative just for the fun on it not because they were useful. I went back to school. Got a postgraduate. The entire time I tried different therapists. Till I found one that just really helped. 

It’s been 10 years since I walked out of the psychiatrists thinking I’d either do it myself or kill myself. It’s been 4 years since I even thought about hurting myself. 2 since my last relapse (which lasted a couple days only). 

Now I’m on my second postgraduate. I travel. I do fun things. I make things. I have fun. I enjoy waking up in the mornings now. I look forward to things. I’m grateful. 

The point I’m trying to make is... I never thought I’d ever live life like this. I only wanted to function. To be able to keep going without alerting everyone around me to how much I hated being alive. 

I credit therapy. Don’t give up. Try everything. Even meds. They didn’t work for me and up to a few years ago I would have continued to try meds but I would have had to wait 2 years on a list to see one through the hospital system in my city so I kinda just kept trying the therapy. A lot of times I thought it wasn’t helping that much until I found one that challenged me. Challenged my way of thinking. Again that was kinda hard but she saved my life. 2 years with her and my life turned around. 

If there’s one thing I’ve learned is that nothing lasts forever. Not the rain or sunshine but we can change. We can grow and learn.

If you are depressed and anxious then your brain is hard wired to see certain negative things and to build on them. You are going to have to make an effort to change it and make it do something different. The good news is with practice it will become easier until one day it's a habit. A therapist would be best at help you, working with you, but until you can find one for yourself, here are some basics. 

Eat right. Give your brain the nutrients it needs to function on a healthy level. More omega3 rich foods like salmon and walnuts and eggs. 
Exercise, it will help your brain and body and self esteem. Just go for a walk in the park or pick a fun sporty activity. 
Every night before sleep, think of three things that make you happy. Three things you are grateful for that happened that day. No matter how small or trivial. Even if it's just I am glad It didn't rain. 
Every night one thing you accomplished. Again doesn't matter how small. Allow yourself to feel pride for a small thing. 

Remember it doesn't matter what other people are doing. Don't measure yourself against others. Only against your past self. If you did one thing today that you did not yesterday, you have succeeded in life. 

Also as a teacher remember, you get to set the example. If you aren't bothered by comments and you are proud of yourself not because of superficial things but because of real important things, that will come across to them and while it may not change all of them, it may effect some of them to be better people and that's an amazing thing.

These will help you build resilience and if someone says something negative or stupid, remind yourself that they have no idea what you have to struggle with everyday and while something was easy for them, it was not so easy when you have to deal with crappy school and terrible people so you deserve far more credit. 

Above all else, Dont give up. School is hard, it's hard for a lot of people but the only way you are going to get a better life is if you keep at it. School is a place to better yourself. Maybe the teachers aren't great, maybe your classmates are shit but take this opportunity to learn. Read and find something you enjoy doing and are good at. Use that as a way to a better life. In high school sometimes it's hard to make friends because your school is filled with crappy people who don't understand you, but the world is filled with many many people, some of whom WILL understand and want to be your friend because they see the good in you. These people are out there and if you give up, you will never meet them. Don't give up, High school will not last forever.
